narrative:
The model predicted a 72.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three academic factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school was the strongest reason the model leaned toward failure. Placing in the fourth decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students, signaled that your grades had not reached the level most successful applicants achieve later in their studies. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most influential factor; at 3.00 it sat below the 3.23 average of those who were admitted, pulling the prediction further toward failure. Your first-year law school performance ranked third. Ranking in the fifth decile compared with an average of sixth among accepted students added another modest push in the same direction.

None of these factors suggested you were likely to pass on the first try. Your LSAT score of 35, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time were less decisive and did not outweigh the academic signals.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue a graduate program, aim to raise your GPA and class ranking, and consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate higher aptitude. These steps would directly address the areas that most influenced this outcome. (218 words)
